title: The ‘impossible triangle’ can’t exist as a solid, yet sculptures fake it from one spot

cover.alt: A polished stainless steel sculpture of an impossible triangle standing on one corner against a blue backdrop.

body: The Penrose triangle looks like three square beams joined at right angles into a closed loop, and every corner seems believable on its own. But taken together they describe a shape that cannot exist as a solid in ordinary three-dimensional space. The Swedish artist Oscar Reutersvärd drew the first one in 1934, and Lionel Penrose and his son Roger, later a Nobel-winning mathematician, came up with it independently and published it in the *British Journal of Psychology* in 1958. Sculptors get around the impossibility with shapes that only line up from one viewpoint; step aside and the ‘triangle’ falls apart.

slides.alt: Three photos side by side of a white sculpture on a roundabout in East Perth: from two angles it is an open, bent shape; from the third it looks like a closed impossible triangle.
slides.caption: Impossible Triangle by Brian McKay and Ahmad Abas, East Perth, 1999. Only from the right angle does it match the flat drawing.

events.text: Oscar Reutersvärd draws the first impossible triangle
Lionel Penrose and his son Roger publish it in a psychology journal
M. C. Escher uses it in his lithograph Waterfall
A giant version goes up on a roundabout in East Perth

slides.heading: Why the eye accepts it
slides.text: Each corner, seen alone, is a perfectly ordinary join of two beams, and the figure can be built up from parts that make sense separately. The contradiction only appears when you follow a beam all the way round. Roger Penrose called it ‘impossibility in its purest form’.

slides.question: The 1958 paper was co-written by Lionel Penrose. What was his profession?
slides.explanation: Lionel Penrose was a psychiatrist and his son Roger a mathematician. Their paper called impossible objects ‘a special type of visual illusion’.

slides.clue: Another name for the Penrose triangle: three bars that can’t be built
slides.detail: The Penrose tribar. Its surface can be bent, without stretching, into five-dimensional space, but never built as a solid in ordinary 3D.
